f: bright red in color
sharing one opinion
living under one roof
r: Latin cōnsanguineus, from con- “together” + sanguis “blood”
s: Am not I consanguineous? am I not of her blood?

f: a spoken (but not necessarily public) declaration of faith made before a congregation
a written (but not necessarily signed) record of a meeting held by church elders
a sudden (but not necessarily lasting) loss of religious belief in a devout person
r: Late Latin theophania, from Greek theós “God” + phaínō “to shine, appear”
s: It was a bewildering theophany, since it was impossible to make out anything clearly in the stormy obscurity of thunder, lightning, smoke and wind.

f: a small lean-to built against a castle wall as a stable
a heavy wagon pulled through the Alps to haul supplies
a narrow canal dug through the marshes as a trade route
r: French caraque, from Latin carrus “wagon”; or perhaps from Arabic qarāqīr
s: Thereafter huge sailing carracks brought Indian pepper and cotton, Indonesian perfume and spice, Chinese silk and porcelain, to the royal trading house at Lisbon.

f: a man’s fur or leather cap
a child’s wool or cotton mitten
a priest’s gold or silver chalice
r: Spanish mantilla “large veil; small cape”, from manta “blanket, cloth”
s: The Duchess of Alba wrapped herself in a mantilla coat.

f: small figure made of carved stone that stands guard in a garden to bring good luck
brief saying or maxim that is engraved on a coin or medal to honor a ruler
curved blade attached to the end of a pole that is used to prune high branches
r: Greek gnṓmōn “discerner, interpreter; carpenter’s square”
s: The little style or gnomon, which being fixed on the pole of the globe, and turning round with it, points out the hours upon the hour circle.

f: full of garlic
gripping by the throat
fond of fine clothing
r: Latin garrulus “talkative”, from garriō “to chatter”
s: She lingered for a few moments, and was garrulous over some detail of the household.

f: lasting for a long time
gloomy and overcast
hard to see through
r: Latin obdūrātus “hardened”, from ob- “against” + dūrō “to harden”
s: But custom maketh blind and obdurate The loftiest hearts.

f: having the habit of turning toward the sun
having the shape of a coiled spiral shell
having the power to cure fever and chills
r: Greek apotrópaios, from apó “away” + trópos “turn”: “turning away evil”
s: A boring subtext, about the wisdom or otherwise of actually uttering Voldemort's name, meanwhile robs the apotropaic device of its force.

f: prone to angry swearing; foul-mouthed and rude
moving along a flowing path; winding and graceful
relating to the healing of illness; medicinal
r: Latin cursorius “hasty, of a race or running”
s: Most junk mail requires only a cursory glance.

f: (of winds) blowing in sudden gusts
(of fabric) wound around the head
(of soil) heavy with peat
r: Latin turbidus “disturbed”, from turba “tumult, disturbance”
s: This makes the estimation of the refractive index of the turbid liquid quite problematic.

f: a layer of fossil fuel trapped in rock (especially beneath an ancient seabed)
a sweet resin that hardens into amber (especially along northern coasts)
a large boulder carried by glaciers (especially one left standing alone on a plain)
r: French pétroglyphe, from Greek pétra “rock” + gluphḗ “carved work”
s: The petroglyphs of Central Asia form a long sequence from the Neolithic onwards.

f: a person who serves in the army without being paid
a person who writes many long books on one subject
a person who studies the eruptions of volcanoes
r: Late Latin voluptuārius, from Latin voluptās “delight, pleasure”
s: Another Greek, the historian Megacleides, singles out Heracles as the supreme voluptuary.

f: overgrown, especially with regard to weeds
underfed, especially with regard to newborn animals
overcast, especially with regard to winter skies
r: Middle English overweninge: overween + -ing
s: She wins one modeling contest in Montana and suddenly she’s overweening.

f: a woven grass mat from the Sahel that is used to shade the doorways of mud houses during the dry season
a stringed instrument from the Sahara that is played by wandering poets at weddings and festivals
a tall headdress from the Sahara that is worn by camel drivers to protect the face from sand
r: Twi (Akan) haramata
s: Okonkwo's fame had grown like a bush-fire in the harmattan.

f: a sudden chill
a Roman tax
a narrow crack
r: Latin rictus
s: His face was a rictus of sheer delight.

f: penal; commonly imposed or carried out as a punishment for minor offenses
rotten; commonly found or left to decay in damp and airless places
graceful; commonly praised or admired for its smooth and polished finish
r: Latin putātīvus “supposed, purported”, from putō “to think, consider”
s: In answer to the objection, that if a thing is only putative, it is fictitious.

f: someone who travels without paying fares (as on trains)
someone who repairs boots and shoes (as in villages)
someone who frees prisoners for ransom (as in feudal times)
r: Dutch vrijbuiter “free booty-er”; a doublet of filibuster
s: The time-honoured connection between forest and freebooter.

f: a poison made from snake venom
a small brass drum (usually Turkish)
a toast to the bride
r: Old Occitan tocasenh, from tocar “strike, touch” + senh “bell”
s: I'll ring the tocsin, I'll have Saint-Antoine out.

f: rich in meat and eggs
lasting through many ages
leaning slightly forward
r: Proteus + -an, after the Greek sea god who could change his shape
s: An amoeba is a protean animalcule.

f: (of the voice) loud and booming as from a great hall
(of the voice) flat and dull as from long repetition
(of the voice) smooth and rich as from careful training
r: Latin tremulus, from tremō “to tremble, shake”
s: The trying nature of his position drove the blood from his cheek, and made his lips tremulous.

f: a secret sign used by members of a society (often a gesture or a handshake)
a small cog or gear in a clockwork mechanism (often made of brass)
a personal motto inscribed on a coat of arms (often written in Latin)
r: Latin cognōmen, from con- “with” + nōmen “name”
s: Gaius was his praenomen or forename, Iulius his nomen or surname, and Caesar his cognomen.

f: so wasteful of money or goods as to bring ruin upon oneself
so clever at an early age as to astonish one’s elders
so precise in manners and speech as to seem stiff
r: Latin prōdigiōsus “strange, marvellous”, from prōdigium “omen, portent, wonder”
s: A prodigious quantity of insects of all sorts (but no mosquitoes) assailed us at our evening meal.

f: eager to question and examine things especially unfamiliar customs or beliefs
tending to agree and comply readily especially with requests from those in authority
able to hear and distinguish sounds especially very faint or distant noises
r: Latin acquīsītus “acquired, gained”
s: She has an acquisitive nature.

f: a small boat (especially one used by fishermen to set crab traps in shallow bayous)
a spicy stew (especially one made with shellfish and served over rice at festivals)
a rowdy dance (especially one held in a barn to celebrate the end of the harvest)
r: Louisiana French, from Spanish la ñapa, from Quechua yapa “addition, increase”
s: Call it a little lagniappe, goodbuddy.

f: a long pole with a sharp blade carried by foot soldiers in medieval armies
a formal assembly of nobles and clergy summoned by a king to approve taxes
a small sitting room set aside for receiving guests in a large house
r: Anglo-Norman parlance, from parler “to talk” + -ance
s: We approach the contest, still known in the common parlance of the country, as "the first Pennimite War."

f: a vessel used for washing; a basin of metal or stone set before guests at a feast
a servant who carves meat; an attendant who waits at the high table during a banquet
a soldier who guards a castle; a man who keeps watch on the walls during the night
r: Medieval Latin vassallus “manservant, retainer”, from Gaulish *wassos “young man, squire”
s: The king ordered his vassals to join him on the crusade unless they had a written note signed by the archbishop or pope.

f: sadness resulting from the loss of a loved one
rudeness resulting from a lack of proper upbringing
wealth resulting from a large inheritance
r: Latin indolentia “freedom from pain; insensibility”
s: Her whole figure expressed a tense vibrant life in singular contrast to the apparent indolence of the men at whom she was talking.

f: marked by an excess of formal politeness or ceremony; bowing and scraping at every turn
marked by dry, barren, or lifeless landscapes; stretching on without water or shade
marked by a deep sense of guilt or regret; brooding over one past mistake
r: Latin dēsultōrius “hasty, superficial”, from dēsultor “a circus rider who jumped from horse to horse”
s: I teach a class of desultory minds.

f: required by law in every case
fond of strict routines and habits
cruel enough to cause harm to others
r: necessity + -ous, after Middle French nécessiteux
s: But it is to be given to our necessitous kindred, or in charity.

f: a sour liquid made from wine or cider used to pickle vegetables or dress salads at home
a climbing plant grown against a wall or trellis to shade a terrace or courtyard
a narrow strip of stained glass set into a church window to depict a saint
r: French vitrine, from vitre “pane of glass”, from Latin vitrum “glass”
s: The dealer was trying to concentrate on showing Bouck some small art-glass pieces in a vitrine in the middle of the booth.

f: relating to the right to use another’s property
tending to take power by force
commonly done or accepted as normal
r: usury + -ous
s: The originator of a usurious loan in California is subject to severe civil penalties.

f: neat and orderly
small and sharp
fond of nesting
r: nettle + -some
s: My old car is very nettlesome.

f: a long walk through rough country
a three-legged frame for a camera
a slow rise in the price of grain
r: Latin trepidātiō, from trepidō “be agitated”
s: I decided, with considerable trepidation, to let him drive my car without me.

f: marked by sudden bursts of great energy
marked by a strong and lasting impact
marked by careless and untidy dress
r: Latin effētus “exhausted”, literally “that has given birth”
s: Most writers merely produce effete works on paper, you might say, but Kerouac went and wrestled with the tree itself.
